claims.text: Template-assisted dealloying can produce high-entropy-alloy three-dimensional nanoframeworks.
Selective dissolution removes less noble elements from an alloy precursor.
Selective dissolution leaves a porous, high-surface-area structure enriched in noble metals.
The precursor contains both noble and less noble metals in a high-entropy configuration.
A sacrificial or removable nanotemplate is applied during dealloying.
Controlled chemical etching selectively removes the less noble components.
The process is performed in an acidic or alkaline chemically controlled environment at elevated temperature and a controlled dealloying rate.
The processing conditions preserve atomic-level disorder in the residual noble-metal network.
The nanotemplate directs formation of a three-dimensional interconnected network.
Dealloying-induced nanopores maintain the high-entropy structure.
The remaining noble-metal atoms self-organize into an interconnected nanoframework.
The resulting nanoframework preserves high-entropy characteristics and exposes a large surface area.
The process produces a three-dimensional nanoframework with a high density of nanopores and a maintained high-entropy-alloy composition.
The template-assisted nanoframework has improved catalytic activity relative to non-templated, conventionally synthesized materials.
Traditional synthesis without templating or dealloying generally yields less controlled porosity and lower accessible surface area.
Effective formation requires chemical-potential differences sufficient for selective dissolution without framework collapse.
The template must withstand dealloying conditions without degrading prematurely.
